A blade is something that is thin, flat, and usually longer than it is wide — like a strip or a sliver. Think of a flat piece of metal, a leaf of grass, or the wing of a fan. That flat, slim shape is what ties all the meanings of "blade" together.

1. The Cutting Part of a Tool or Weapon

This is the most familiar meaning. The blade is the thin, sharpened edge of anything designed to cut. It is the part that does the actual cutting — not the handle, not the body, just that sharp, flat piece.

  • A knife blade is the flat metal part you use to slice.
  • A sword blade is the long, sharp strip of metal, as opposed to the handle (called the hilt).
  • A razor blade is the ultra-thin strip of metal that shaves hair.
  • A scalpel blade is what a surgeon uses to make precise cuts.
  • A saw blade is the flat, toothed strip that cuts through wood or metal.
  • A mower blade spins beneath a lawn mower and cuts the grass.
  • A blender blade is the small, sharp, spinning piece inside a blender.

The key idea here: a blade is the working, cutting part of a sharp instrument — precise, thin, and flat.

2. A Flat, Thin Part of a Machine or Device (Not Necessarily Sharp)

The word "blade" is also used for flat, wing-like parts of machines that move air, water, or other forces — even when they are not sharp at all. Here, the shape (flat and elongated) is what matters, not the sharpness.

  • A fan blade is one of the flat arms that spin to push air around a room.
  • A helicopter blade (or rotor blade) is the long, flat arm that spins on top of a helicopter and lifts it into the air.
  • A propeller blade is one of the flat, curved arms of a ship or airplane's propeller.
  • A turbine blade is a flat fin inside a turbine engine that is pushed by steam, gas, or water to generate power.
  • A windshield wiper blade is the flat rubber strip that sweeps rain off a car's windshield.
  • An oar blade or paddle blade is the flat, wide end of an oar or paddle that dips into the water.

3. A Single Leaf of Grass

This meaning might surprise you, but it is very common and natural in English. A blade of grass means a single, narrow leaf of a grass plant — that thin, flat, green strip that pokes up from the ground.

You almost always hear it this way: "a blade of grass" (singular). It is rarely said in any other form unless you are talking about many of them.

"She lay on the lawn, staring up at the sky, pulling at a blade of grass."

"After the drought, there wasn't a single blade of grass left in the yard."

The shape connection is clear: a grass leaf is thin, flat, and long — just like a blade.

4. The Flat Part of Any Plant Leaf (Botanical Sense)

In a slightly more technical but still common sense, the "blade" of a leaf refers to the broad, flat, main part of the leaf — as opposed to the stalk (the thin stem that connects the leaf to the branch). If you look at a maple leaf, the wide, flat section with all the veins is the blade. The narrow stalk connecting it to the tree is not.

This meaning is most common in gardening, biology, and botany, but you may also encounter it in everyday conversation about plants.

5. The Metal Runner on an Ice Skate

In the context of ice skating, the blade refers to the thin strip of metal fixed to the bottom of an ice skate — the part that makes contact with the ice and allows the skater to glide.

"She fell and bent one of her blades."

"He took his skates to the shop to get the blades sharpened."

Skaters often refer to their skates simply as their "blades" as a shorthand.

6. The Shoulder Blade (Anatomy)

You have likely heard the phrase "shoulder blade" — this refers to the large, flat, triangular bone at the back of your shoulder. Its scientific name is the scapula, but in everyday English, everyone calls it the shoulder blade.

The name comes from the shape: it is flat, broad, and thin — just like a blade.

"She pulled a muscle near her shoulder blade."

More broadly in anatomy, doctors and scientists sometimes use "blade" to describe any flat, wide bone or flat section of a bone, though "shoulder blade" is by far the most common everyday use.

7. The Blade of a Skate (Inline / Roller Skates)

Just as with ice skates, the wheels and frame on the bottom of inline skates (also called rollerblades) are sometimes referred to as the blade — referring to the elongated, flat undercarriage. This is where the brand name "Rollerblades" comes from.

8. A Dashing, Lively Young Man (Old-Fashioned / Archaic)

This meaning is old-fashioned and rarely used in modern speech, but you may come across it in older literature or historical texts. A blade was an informal word for a bold, spirited, fashionable young man — someone who was lively, adventurous, and a bit daring.

"He was quite the blade in his youth — always at parties, always charming everyone."

The most famous phrase from this era is "a gay blade," where gay means cheerful and lively (not its modern meaning). You might see this in classic novels or period films. It is essentially a compliment meaning a fun, energetic, stylish man.

Every use of "blade" comes back to the same underlying picture: something thin, flat, and elongated. Whether it cuts (a knife blade), spins (a fan blade), grows (a blade of grass), slides (a skate blade), or simply exists as bone (a shoulder blade) — the word always evokes that slim, flat shape. Once you see that shape in your mind, the word "blade" will feel intuitive no matter which context you encounter it in.
Common Collocations and Phrases to Know

These are fixed word combinations that native speakers use naturally:

  • blade of grass — a single grass leaf (the most common phrasing)
  • shoulder blade — the flat back bone
  • razor blade — a sharp, thin metal strip for shaving
  • saw blade — the cutting strip of a saw
  • fan blade / rotor blade / propeller blade — flat arms of spinning machines
  • the blade of a knife/sword/dagger — the sharp, flat cutting part
  • skate blades — the metal runners of ice skates
  • a gay blade — (old-fashioned) a dashing, spirited young man

ContextWhat "blade" means

In everyday use, blade most commonly means the sharp, flat cutting part of a knife, sword, or similar tool. In machines and technology, it means a flat, paddle-like arm (fan, propeller, turbine). In nature, it means a single narrow leaf of grass, or the wide flat part of any leaf. In anatomy, it refers to the flat shoulder bone. In skating, it is the metal runner underfoot. And in old-fashioned literature, it means a lively, stylish young man.
